+        vocab = {idx: bytes([idx]) for idx in range(256)} # idx -> bytes
+        # count the number of times every consecutive pair appears, once;
+        # where maps each pair to the indices of the chunks containing it
+        stats = {}
+        where = {}
+        for j, (chunk_ids, w) in enumerate(zip(ids, weights)):
+            for cpair in zip(chunk_ids, chunk_ids[1:]):
+                stats[cpair] = stats.get(cpair, 0) + w
+                if cpair in where:
+                    where[cpair].add(j)
+                else:
+                    where[cpair] = {j}
+        for i in range(num_merges):
+            if not stats:
+                raise ValueError("max() arg is an empty sequence")
+            # find the pair with the highest count; ties go to the pair
+            # that occurs first in chunk order
+            top = max(stats.values())
+            tied = [p for p, c in stats.items() if c == top]
+            if len(tied) == 1:
+                cpair = tied[0]
+            else:
+                first = min(min(where[p]) for p in tied)
+                tied = set(tied)
+                chunk_ids = ids[first]
+                cpair = next(p for p in zip(chunk_ids, chunk_ids[1:]) if p in tied)
+            pair = (ord(cpair[0]), ord(cpair[1]))
+            # mint a new token: assign it the next available id
+            idx = 256 + i
+            # replace all occurrences of pair in the affected chunks with idx
+            # (str.replace is left to right and non-overlapping),
+            # updating the pair counts of those chunks only
+            old = cpair[0] + cpair[1]
+            new = chr(idx)
+            for j in sorted(where[cpair]):
+                chunk_ids = ids[j]
+                w = weights[j]
+                new_ids = chunk_ids.replace(old, new)
+                ids[j] = new_ids
+                for p in zip(chunk_ids, chunk_ids[1:]):
+                    stats[p] -= w
+                for p in zip(new_ids, new_ids[1:]):
+                    if p in stats:
+                        stats[p] += w
+                    else:
+                        stats[p] = w
+                old_pairs = set(zip(chunk_ids, chunk_ids[1:]))
+                new_pairs = set(zip(new_ids, new_ids[1:]))
+                for p in old_pairs - new_pairs:
+                    where[p].discard(j)
+                    if not stats[p]:
+                        del stats[p]
+                        del where[p]
+                for p in new_pairs - old_pairs:
+                    if p in where:
+                        where[p].add(j)
+                    else:
+                        where[p] = {j}

actions.reason: RegexTokenizer.train recounted every adjacent pair across all distinct chunks on each merge. Now the pair counts are built once, together with an index from each pair to the chunks that contain it. Each merge only touches the chunks that hold the merged pair: their old pair counts are subtracted, str.replace is applied, and their new pair counts are added. The index is kept exact. Ties are broken as before, by the first occurrence in chunk order (the insertion order of the old recount): the earliest chunk holding a tied pair is taken from the index and only that chunk is scanned. If no pairs are left, the same ValueError as max() of an empty sequence is raised. Measured: train_regex_ir ratio 0.2644, outputs identical, other metrics within limits.

journal.text:
I rewrote RegexTokenizer.train in minbpe/regex.py, lines 82-99, and changed line 145. The old loop recounted every adjacent pair across all distinct chunks on each merge. Now pair counts are built once, along with an index from each pair to the chunks that contain it. Each merge only touches chunks holding the merged pair. It subtracts their old pair counts, applies str.replace, and adds their new counts.

My sandbox run accepted it with identical outputs. train_regex_ir went from 2108543275 to 557525737, ratio 0.2644. The other metrics moved slightly up. train_basic_ir was 1.0028, encode_ir 1.0007, decode_ir 1.0039 and save_load_ir 1.0044. All were within guard limits. The guard reported 1 file, 64 lines.

The full recount was the main cost in regex training. Incremental counts remove most of it. The small rises elsewhere were not touched by this edit and look like noise. The verdict waits on replays.

Next, check whether tie breaking matches the parent on other inputs. After that, look at encode_ir.
